editor_spans.body: The Motherwell speech adds something the advance briefing didn't have: a firm offer of 'DWP devolution'. That matters because it changes who holds the leverage. Local government in Scotland is already devolved, so Westminster can't hand Scottish regions power over councils. Employment support is mostly reserved to Westminster, though, so it is something the Prime Minister actually has to give. The same goes for the innovation, enterprise and employability funding he says the UK might devolve, and for the research and development money he wants Scotland's regions to help direct.

The offer comes with conditions on how Holyrood would use it. The model is to be 'shaped by Holyrood', but it 'has to be based on the Easterhouse principle... If it's not based on that, it won't work.' It also has to reach down to the regions, not stop in Edinburgh. So Westminster would hand over a reserved power while setting the terms for how the Scottish Government delivers it. That makes this less a straight transfer than a test: a refusal, or a Holyrood-run scheme that stays centralised, would make the Scottish Government look like the bottleneck. That is the trap the briefing hinted at, and now there is something specific for it to close on.

The speech never spells out what 'DWP devolution' covers. The 2016 Scotland Act already devolved some employment programmes for disabled and long-term unemployed people. Jobcentres, Universal Credit and the rules on what claimants must do to keep their benefits stayed with Westminster. Devolving more programme money is a small step. Devolving the jobcentres and work coaches would be a constitutional change. The speech's tone points two ways. 'Names not numbers' and Darren McGarvey's book Poverty Safari suggest a gentler system. The line 'I won't have a country where we get comfortable with the idea of kids in their 20s just being there on benefits' and the Milburn review suggest a tougher one. Which of those Holyrood would be asked to run is the question that matters most.

There is a reason for building the pitch around Easterhouse. By saying he took a Glasgow estate's idea to Greater Manchester and is now offering to bring it home, the Prime Minister answers the usual charge that Westminster imposes its own models on Scotland. He presents it as Scotland's own idea coming back. His career story does similar work: he is cast as a fellow victim of Whitehall, not its representative.

Story 437, the Editor's, made 2026-10-24: "The biggest line of the week sits in the middle of a Commons statement about the UN. After the 20 November summit, the Prime Minister wants a 'serious dialogue about the different options' for the long-term relationship with the EU. He says the status quo is 'not good enough' and that 'the British public will be the boss'. That is a deliberately vague way to reopen the question of how close Britain should be to Europe, and it leaves room for a future public vote without ever saying 'referendum'. It fits his other moves this week: in Scotland, on the railways and in Europe, his answer is to rebuild institutions, not adjust policy at the edges."; cited by no later Editor's Span

  · The Great British Railways headquarters story is mostly about timing. Building at Becketwell starts in early 2027 and is due to finish by spring 2029, around the deadline for the next general election. Its permanent home and the political cycle will end at roughly the same moment. The headline 'hundreds of rail jobs' rests on a building for up to 450 staff, and the release never says how many of those posts are new and how many are existing railway staff moving to Derby.
  S368 (the Editor's): The figure buried in the release matters more than the HQ: less than 7% of the railway's workforce is under 25. Up to 600 apprentices over four years, roughly 150 a year across the national network, is a small answer to an ageing workforce. It is also paid for from the general youth employment package rather than as rail workforce planning. Bringing the railway into public ownership means the state now owns this skills problem too.
